definition: Someone who dabbles in an art or field without serious study or lasting commitment.
example: Her uncle was a dilettante who took up pottery, chess and Italian, then quit each within a month.
nuance: An amateur may be deeply skilled and devoted, but a dilettante's interest is shallow and often more for show than mastery.
prompt: A music teacher describes a student who keeps switching instruments.
options: A true dilettante, Marco tried violin, drums and flute but never stuck with one.
As a dilettante, Marco has practiced the cello every morning for ten straight years.
The conservatory named Marco its leading dilettante for his flawless mastery of the oboe.
Marco felt like a nervous dilettante at his first formal society ball in a new suit.
reasons: Sampling many instruments without committing to any is exactly what dabbling looks like.
A decade of daily practice shows deep commitment, the reverse of casual dabbling.
Flawless mastery marks an expert; the word suggests shallow skill and is rarely an honor.
A first society ball suggests the look-alike "debutante," which has nothing to do with dabbling.

practice.prompt: Guests at a dinner party start talking about philosophy.
options: The dilettante, a professor who had studied ethics for forty years, explained each argument in depth.
The dilettante arrived two hours late to dinner because he habitually put off every task.
Guests praised the dilettante as the most rigorous and disciplined thinker they had ever met.
The dilettante quoted famous philosophers but had read only the back covers of their books.
reasons: Forty years of scholarly study is expertise, not superficial dabbling.
Chronic delay fits the look-alike "dilatory"; the word is about shallow interest, not lateness.
The word usually implies a lack of rigor, so it can't sensibly name the most disciplined thinker.
Showing off knowledge picked up from book covers is the surface-level interest the word describes.
